title: Zelophehad's Daughters and the Tribe's Inheritance
summary: The leaders of the clan of Gilead, in the tribe of Manasseh, raise a problem with the earlier ruling for Zelophehad's daughters: if the women marry into other tribes, their land will pass out of Manasseh. At the LORD's word Moses rules that heiresses must marry within their father's tribe, so that no inheritance moves from tribe to tribe. The five daughters marry cousins on their father's side, and the book of Numbers closes with a summary of the commands given on the plains of Moab.
story: Numbers ends where the second half of the book began, with the daughters of Zelophehad. In chapter 27 they asked for their father's land and God granted it. Now their own clan asks a follow-up question, and God answers again. The book that began with the ordering of the tribes around the tabernacle at Sinai ends with a ruling that keeps each tribe's land intact, and with five women doing as the LORD commanded. After forty years of grumbling and rebellion, the book's last narrative scene is one of quiet obedience. The story continues in Deuteronomy, where Moses addresses the whole people on the same plains of Moab, and in Joshua, where the daughters receive their land (Joshua 17:3-6).
historical:
The clan of Gilead, descended from Machir son of Manasseh, was one of the leading clans of its tribe. Part of Manasseh settled east of the Jordan in Gilead and Bashan (32:39-42), and part west of the Jordan in the central hill country, where Zelophehad's daughters would receive their land. The book of Joshua records that Manasseh's western territory included portions for the daughters (Joshua 17:3-6). As noted in chapter 27, several of their names match place names known in that region, including Tirzah, which later served as a royal city of the northern kingdom.

The mention of the Jubilee (verse 4) refers to the law of Leviticus 25, under which land sold during the previous fifty years returned to its original family in the fiftieth year. The clan leaders worry that the Jubilee would not help them: if land passed to another tribe by marriage rather than by sale, it would stay there permanently. The Old Testament gives little evidence of how fully the Jubilee was ever practiced, but the law expressed the principle that the land belonged to God and that families held it as his tenants (Leviticus 25:23).
cultural:
Land in ancient Israel was the foundation of a family's life and identity. A family's fields fed it, provided its place in the community, and carried its name forward. Tribal territory held the same meaning on a larger scale. Marriage normally moved a woman into her husband's family, and any property she brought went with her. If an heiress married outside her tribe, her father's land would become part of her husband's tribe's inheritance, and over time tribal boundaries could be eroded.

Marriage between cousins was common and accepted in the ancient Near East, and it was a customary way to keep property within a family. The ruling does not force the daughters to marry anyone in particular. “They may marry anyone they please”, as long as the husband comes from their father's tribe. The daughters married “cousins on their father’s side”, keeping the land within Manasseh and within their own clan. The approach of the clan leaders shows how legal questions were raised in Israel: by elders speaking for their clans, bringing their concern to Moses, who sought the LORD's word.
literary: The chapter is a short legal narrative, parallel to 27:1-11. There, the daughters brought a case and God said they “speak correctly”; here, the clan leaders bring a related case, and Moses says, “The tribe of the sons of Joseph speaks correctly.” The same phrase affirms both sides, and the two rulings fit together. The daughters' names are listed again in verse 11, in a slightly different order from 26:33 and 27:1. The final verse (13) is a colophon, a closing note summarizing a section of text, which frames everything from chapter 22 onward as the commandments given on the plains of Moab, by the Jordan across from Jericho. That phrase echoes 22:1 and gives the last part of Numbers its setting.

outline.t: The clan of Gilead raises a concern about the inheritance
Heiresses must marry within their father's tribe
Closing summary of the commands given in Moab

doctrines.note: Each tribe's land was part of God's covenant gift, and the law protects that gift from being scattered. The inheritance of the tribes was meant to endure as a sign that God's promise was permanent.

The law is applied and refined through real cases. The first ruling for the daughters raised a new question, and God gave a further ruling that balanced the rights of the daughters with the needs of the tribe.
The chapter shows how closely family, land, and faith were bound together in Israel. The daughters' marriages were part of keeping faith with their father's name and their tribe's inheritance.

words.note: Nachalah, inheritance. The word appears seventeen times in this short chapter, more densely than anywhere else in Numbers. Its repetition shows the issue at stake: each tribe's inheritance must remain its own. The book that has spoken so much of death in the wilderness ends by speaking of inheritance in the land.

Matteh, tribe. The word also means staff or rod, and it may have come to mean tribe because a leader's staff represented his tribe (as with the twelve staffs of chapter 17). In this chapter it appears again and again as the ruling protects each tribe's territory.

Davaq, to cling or hold fast. In verses 7 and 9 each tribe is to hold fast to its inheritance. It is the same verb used in Genesis 2:24 for a man clinging to his wife and in Deuteronomy for Israel clinging to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20). It conveys loyalty and close attachment.

christ: The concern of this chapter is that the inheritance should not be lost, and the New Testament speaks of an inheritance that cannot be lost at all. Peter describes it as “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4). Paul says that believers are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17), and that the Spirit is the guarantee of the inheritance (Ephesians 1:14). In Christ the boundaries between tribes no longer divide God's people, since Jew and Gentile alike share in the promise (Ephesians 3:6). The link is one of fulfillment on a larger scale: the land kept within each tribe points to a people whose inheritance is kept by God himself.
questions: The daughters of Zelophehad appear at the start of their case and at its end, and in between the law was clarified twice. What does their story teach about raising honest questions in a community of faith?
The book of Numbers, full of rebellion, ends with a scene of simple obedience. Why might that be a fitting ending for this book?
The chapter is concerned that the inheritance of each tribe not be lost. What do you think it means to hold fast to what God has entrusted to you?
